issues.legal_issue: A landlord must determine a contractual tenancy before suing to recover possession for non-payment of rent.
material_facts: The tenant occupied the premises under a contractual tenancy.
The landlords sued for ejectment on the ground of non-payment of rent under the rent-control legislation.
The landlords had served a notice to quit, which the court found valid and effective to determine the tenancy.
issues.conclusion: Determination of the contractual tenancy was a prerequisite to the suit. The notice to quit validly determined the tenancy, so the landlords could bring the suit for recovery of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 106 and 111(b) of the Transfer of Property Act, a contractual lease must be determined by a legally effective mode, including a valid notice to quit, before the landlord becomes entitled to possession. Section 12 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 restricts recovery of possession after that right arises; it does not itself create a right to evict or displace the ordinary law governing determination of the tenancy. The court relied on Dr. K. A. Dhairyawan v. J. R. Thakur, Raghubir Narayan Lotlikar v. Fernandez, Karsandas v. Karsanji, Meghji Lakhamahi and Brothers v. Furniture Workshop, and Ebner v. Lascelles, and distinguished Rai Brij Raj Krishna v. S. K. Shaw and Brothers and Shri Hem Chand v. Shrimati Sham Devi.

predicates.landlord_seeks_recovery_from_tenant: A landlord has brought a proceeding to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_is_contractual: The tenant's possession rests on a contractual tenancy rather than solely on a statutory right to remain in possession.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks possession from a tenant under a contractual tenancy, the tenancy must first be determined.

issues.legal_issue: A law requiring rent to be recovered according to a different calendar does not, without more, change the calendar governing the tenancy or invalidate a notice to quit aligned with the original calendar.
material_facts: The tenancy was originally arranged by reference to the Indian Calendar.
The notice to quit required the tenant to leave on the last day of a month under that calendar.
The applicable rent-control provisions and rule required rent to be recovered according to the British Calendar but did not change the calendar governing the tenancy.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy continued to be governed by the Indian Calendar, and the notice to quit was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 and rule 4 provided for the calculation and recovery of rent according to the British Calendar; neither provision converted the contractual period of the tenancy to that calendar. A change in the calendar used to recover rent does not, without a specific provision, alter the tenancy period fixed by the parties.

predicates.notice_to_quit_dispute: A party disputes whether a notice to quit validly ended a tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_uses_original_calendar: The parties fixed the tenancy period by reference to a particular calendar.
predicates.rent_recovery_uses_different_calendar: A legal requirement uses a different calendar for calculating or recovering rent without expressly changing the tenancy period.

issues.definition: If a notice dispute concerns a tenancy fixed by one calendar while rent recovery uses another, the original calendar continues to govern the tenancy and the notice.

issues.legal_issue: Payment of rent arrears only after an ejectment suit is filed does not prevent or make discretionary an eviction decree when the statutory conditions for eviction for substantial arrears are satisfied.
material_facts: The landlords brought an ejectment suit after the tenant had failed to pay rent despite a demand notice.
The arrears had remained unpaid for the qualifying period, and the standard rent was not disputed.
The tenant deposited arrears in court after the suit had been instituted.
The courts below decreed ejectment, and the Supreme Court upheld the decree.
issues.conclusion: The post-filing payment did not affect the tenant's liability to eviction or the court's power to decree eviction. Once the statutory conditions were satisfied, the court was bound to pass the decree and had no discretion to refuse it.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 12(2) and section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a landlord may sue after the tenant fails to pay within the prescribed time after a demand, and a decree must follow where rent is payable by the month, the qualifying arrears exist, and the tenant has not paid within the time allowed after the demand. Payment after institution of the suit does not undo the basis for eviction. Although section 12(3)(a) uses the word “may,” it does not confer discretion to refuse a decree when its conditions are met; the contrast with section 12(3)(b), which expressly provides a means for a tenant to avoid eviction by paying and continuing to pay, confirms that result. The court also held that section 12 provides no relief against forfeiture in these circumstances.

rule.if: rent_ejectment_proceeding and monthly_rent and qualifying_rent_arrears and standard_rent_undisputed and demand_deadline_passed_without_payment and arrears_paid_only_after_suit_filed

predicates.rent_ejectment_proceeding: A landlord has brought an ejectment proceeding based on non-payment of rent.
predicates.monthly_rent: The rent is payable by the month.
predicates.qualifying_rent_arrears: The tenant has arrears that meet the applicable statutory threshold for eviction.
predicates.standard_rent_undisputed: The tenant has not disputed the amount of standard rent.
predicates.demand_deadline_passed_without_payment: The tenant failed to pay within the time allowed after receiving a demand for the arrears.
predicates.arrears_paid_only_after_suit_filed: The tenant paid or deposited the arrears only after the landlord had instituted the ejectment suit.

issues.definition: When a monthly-rent ejectment proceeding concerns qualifying, undisputed arrears left unpaid after demand and payment occurs only after suit is filed, an eviction decree must issue despite that later payment.
